section_title: What happens to the outward splendor in which Zion takes pride?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 16 The LORD also says: “Because the daughters of Zion are haughty— walking with heads held high and wanton eyes, prancing and skipping as they go, jingling the bracelets on their ankles— 17 the Lord will bring sores on the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will make their foreheads bare.”

18 In that day the Lord will take away their finery: their anklets and headbands and crescents; 19 their pendants, bracelets, and veils; 20 their headdresses, ankle chains, and sashes; their perfume bottles and charms; 21 their signet rings and nose rings; 22 their festive robes, capes, cloaks, and purses; 23 and their mirrors, linen garments, tiaras, and shawls.

24 Instead of fragrance there will be a stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of styled hair, baldness; instead of fine clothing, sackcloth; instead of beauty, shame. 25 Your men will fall by the sword, and your warriors in battle. 26 And the gates of Zion will lament and mourn; destitute, she will sit on the ground.

context_lines: The warning turns to the proud daughters of Zion: their looks, movements and ornaments display the importance they place on appearance. The long list of clothing, jewelry and accessories makes their outward splendor vivid.

The announced judgment reverses that condition. Fragrance gives way to stench, fine dress to sackcloth and styled hair to baldness. The things used to display status cannot protect them from loss and humiliation.

The scene widens to fallen warriors and Zion herself sitting destitute, with her gates mourning. The loss belongs to the disaster overtaking the city, continuing the chapter’s warning against pride and the misuse of advantage.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/3.htm) emphasizes the neglect of devotion, generosity and justice while time and resources are spent on display. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/3.htm) similarly begins with pride as the source of the behavior described.

The [NABRE notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/isaiah/3) place these women within the ruling class and note that many terms in the clothing list are rare and difficult to identify precisely. The overall reversal remains clear even where the exact shape of an accessory is uncertain: the city’s finery will become mourning.
god_plan_lines: The wider question of what God values appears in [1 Peter 3:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/3.htm). Peter directs attention to the enduring beauty of the heart and a gentle spirit precious to God, in a passage where conduct may lead an unbelieving spouse toward faith.

[1 Timothy 2:8–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_timothy/2.htm) joins prayer without anger among men with modesty, self-control and good deeds among women. The connection is a people whose worship becomes visible through character and conduct. Outward display cannot supply the inward faithfulness that makes such a witness possible.
